title: Soft Delete, Restore and Purge Rules
prompt:
A docs app keeps deleted folders in a trash for 30 days. Records are `{ id, slug, parentId, deletedAt }` (`deletedAt` is a day number or `null`). Write `replayTrash(records, ops)` returning `{ log, active }` where `active` is the sorted ids of non-deleted records at the end. Ops, applied in order (never mutate the input):
- `{ type: 'delete', id, at }`: unknown -> `delete X: not found`; already deleted -> `delete X: already deleted`; else set `deletedAt = at` on X and cascade to every active descendant (children by `parentId`, recursively), logging `delete X (+N children)` with N = descendants deleted by this op.
- `{ type: 'restore', id, at }`: checks in order: unknown -> `restore X: not found`; active -> `restore X: not deleted`; `at - deletedAt > 30` -> `restore X: retention expired`; parent exists and is deleted -> `restore X: parent P is deleted`; another active record has the same slug -> `restore X: slug taken by Y` (first such record in array order). Otherwise restore X and, walking down from it, every descendant whose `deletedAt` equals X's old `deletedAt` (they were deleted together). A descendant whose slug is taken by an active record stays deleted, together with its own subtree; count it as skipped. Log `restore X (+N children)` or `restore X (+N children, M skipped)` when M > 0.
- `{ type: 'purge', at }`: permanently remove records with `at - deletedAt > 30`; log `purge: N removed`.

explanation.beginner: Soft delete means 'set a deletedAt date instead of removing the row', so it can be undone. Work on copies of the records. Deleting a folder should also hide everything inside it, so walk down the tree (children are records whose parentId is this id) and stamp them with the same day. That shared stamp is the trick for restoring: when you restore the folder, bring back exactly the children that were deleted in the same action, and leave alone a child that someone deleted on its own earlier. Before restoring, check the rules in the given order - each one prevents a real bug: restoring into a deleted parent makes an orphan you cannot see, and restoring a duplicate slug breaks URLs.
explanation.junior: Model each op as a guard chain that returns the first failure; order matters and is part of the spec. Cascades are tree walks (stack or queue over a children lookup), O(n) per op with a precomputed map, O(n^2) with `filter` as here - fine for small trees. Using `deletedAt` equality as a 'deleted together' marker avoids storing a separate batch id, but it is fragile if two independent deletes share a timestamp; production systems record a deletion batch id. When a cascaded child cannot be restored (slug conflict), do not descend into it - restoring its children would create records under a deleted parent. Retention uses a strict `>` so day 30 is still restorable, and purge applies the same boundary, so tests at exactly 30 days pin that down. Slug uniqueness among active rows is what a partial unique index (`WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`) enforces in SQL.
